messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun is a 20-year-old South Asian male writer, currently single, who was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 72. He presents with a severe and entrenched post-traumatic stress picture that developed in the months following the sudden death of his older brother, Rohan, who collapsed without warning from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia at the age of 24. Rohan had been Arjun's closest confidant and, in many ways, the person around whom Arjun had organised his sense of the future — they had spoken the week before about sharing an apartment once Arjun finished his undergraduate degree. The death came with no warning, no illness, no logic. Rohan had been laughing at dinner and was gone before the ambulance arrived. It was Arjun who had been in the room.

In the weeks that followed, Arjun found that the world he had understood himself to be living in had simply ceased to exist. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that safety was an illusion — that the world was dangerous in a way he had never previously registered, that the ordinary fabric of daily life concealed catastrophic ruptures that could open without notice. These beliefs were not abstract. They sat in his body. He was unable to relax even in environments he knew to be physically safe; what frightened him most was not any specific threat but the felt impossibility of letting his guard down when he now understood, viscerally, that nothing guaranteed the next moment. He startled violently at ordinary sounds — a door closing in the hallway of his apartment, a phone ringing across the room — and his nights were fractured, sleep arriving only briefly before anxiety pulled him back to wakefulness. His nervous system had reorganised itself around a new premise: that danger was ambient and constant.

These shattered beliefs about how the world worked drove Arjun toward a set of strategies that felt, at first, like reasonable self-protection. He stopped making plans. He had been the kind of person who mapped out months in advance — deadlines, trips, ambitions — but any attempt to project himself into the future now produced a nauseating sense of futility. Why plan, when plans assumed a continuity that Rohan's death had proved was not guaranteed? He also began systematically avoiding anything that reminded him of his loss: he stopped listening to the music they had shared, stopped visiting the neighbourhood where they had grown up, and found himself unable to open the folder on his laptop where he had saved Rohan's messages. As a writer, this avoidance carried a particular cost. His work had always drawn on emotional depth and autobiographical resonance, but now whole territories of feeling were cordoned off. He had missed two submission deadlines and withdrawn from a mentorship programme he had worked hard to join. His editor, who had once described him as unusually mature for his age, had begun asking carefully worded questions about whether he was managing. He was not.

Alongside the avoidance, Arjun had developed a pattern of seeking reassurance from friends and family — texting his mother after any period of silence, asking friends repeatedly whether they thought he was coping normally, whether they thought he seemed okay. Yet each reassurance faded within hours, because the underlying conviction that something was irreparably wrong with him and with the world was not touched by it. He had lost the person he used to be — he described this plainly: he used to be happy, and now he was always miserable, and he was no longer sure the earlier version of himself was recoverable. This belief that he was permanently changed fed directly back into the avoidance and the hypervigilance: if he was broken and the world was dangerous, then planning was futile and relaxation was irresponsible, and so the strategies that were meant to protect him instead kept confirming the appraisals that made them feel necessary. The reassurance-seeking left him feeling more dependent and less capable; the avoidance of grief reminders meant the loss was never processed, only circled. His sleep remained poor, his startle response remained hair-trigger, and the sense of safety he had once taken entirely for granted felt further away with each passing week.

What finally brought Arjun to seek help was a conversation with his mother in which she wept and told him she was frightened she was losing him too. He had not realised, until that moment, how visible his withdrawal had become. He arrived at the intake session quiet and precise, choosing his words carefully in the way writers do. What he most feared was that nothing would change. What he most hoped, though he said it almost as an aside, was that it might be possible to remember Rohan without it destroying him.
